title: Recently had a deeper look at the capability of an AI platform (RollOnFriday discussion-board thread)
pub: RollOnFriday, main discussion board (anonymous UK lawyers' forum)
author: Anonymous RollOnFriday discussion-board participants

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The thread substantially supports the cluster’s claim that AI will disrupt labour-intensive production, staffing and fixed-fee economics, while recognising confidentiality, hallucination and data constraints. However, some contributors go materially beyond hybrid, lawyer-supervised delivery and advocate broad substitution of lawyers, so the source does not consistently accept the cluster’s central distinction between challenging production and displacing lawyers.
qs: Having recently been designated our firm’s lead on AI implementation (in my practice area) I have a similar impression to [handle]  The old model of expensive humans expensively sweating and gurning to nobody’s great benefit is dead, and in the round that’s a good thing.
The whole thing should be taken over by AI and the sooner the better.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The thread contains substantive support for AI substituting for document-heavy legal tasks and reshaping staffing and billing, but equally substantive practitioner objections based on errors, verification burdens, confidentiality, workflow fit and uncertain timing. As a multi-participant discussion, it reinforces the cluster’s uncertainty rather than adopting one overall forecast.
qs: Yes some senior and experienced mind may provide a gloss or recommendation on the work product - partner to client board or senior associate to client senior lawyer - but the justification for use of people to crawl over documents and dredge up the evidence is dead.
I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The thread substantively supports the cluster’s emphasis on uneven capabilities, active verification, human supervision, workflow redesign and risks to junior development. However, it also contains strong predictions of broad lawyer substitution, rapid structural collapse and imminent productivity gains that go beyond—and sometimes conflict with—the cluster’s cautious, selective-deployment proposition. Because the source is a multi-participant debate without a clear overall direction, its position is mixed.
qs: From what I have seen there are still many absolute howler errors/hallucinations in the work product and accuracy comparisons to humans are misleading.
The whole thing should be taken over by AI and the sooner the better.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The source supports conditional AI assistance under existing professional duties, court oversight and competent human review. Its quoted Australian guidance also reflects the cluster’s account of disclosure as jurisdiction-specific and potentially required on request rather than universally mandatory. The thread’s pricing and job-loss comments are ancillary and do not alter this overall alignment.
qs: This requires users of Generative AI to be guided by, and act in accordance with, their existing legal and professional responsibilities.[3] It follows that there will be circumstances where it is inappropriate to use Generative AI at all or where users ought to be transparent about its use.
I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: The thread broadly supports the synthesis’s cautious position: it raises the possibility that Claude could displace specialist legal-AI intermediaries, while treating continued human legal responsibility, commercial adoption incentives and reliability problems as important constraints. Its claims are anecdotal and anonymous, so they reinforce the framing rather than establish autonomous practice or actual vendor displacement.
qs: There’s been a lot of talk about whether both are in danger of being replaced directly by Claude as Anthropic have released legal co-working tools themselves.
There’s going to be a human giving legal advice ultimately unless they change the law (which we might protest about!).

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core position that existing professional duties govern AI use and that knowledgeable human review remains necessary. Its quoted court guidance also supports context-sensitive disclosure or non-use rather than a universal disclosure mandate, though it does not materially address sanctions doctrine or inquiry failures.
qs: This requires users of Generative AI to be guided by, and act in accordance with, their existing legal and professional responsibilities.[3] It follows that there will be circumstances where it is inappropriate to use Generative AI at all or where users ought to be transparent about its use.
I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The relevant court guidance and poster commentary align with the cluster’s copilot framing: AI may save time on routine processing, but existing professional duties, context-sensitive limits and competent human review remain essential. The thread’s pricing challenge and unsupported job-loss prediction are peripheral rather than contrary.
qs: This requires users of Generative AI to be guided by, and act in accordance with, their existing legal and professional responsibilities.[3] It follows that there will be circumstances where it is inappropriate to use Generative AI at all or where users ought to be transparent about its use.
I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The thread broadly supports the synthesis’s core: generative AI can save time on bounded, routine legal tasks, but current errors, hallucinations and professional duties make knowledgeable human verification essential. Its contributors disagree on the speed and scale of labour-market and pricing disruption, but those speculative differences are consistent with the cluster’s conclusion that wholesale lawyer replacement and commercial outcomes remain unsettled.
qs: I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.
From what I have seen there are still many absolute howler errors/hallucinations in the work product and accuracy comparisons to humans are misleading.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: The thread supports the synthesis’s contested-platform framing: some posters view specialist products as replaceable wrappers vulnerable to direct Claude competition, while others identify legal workflow tailoring and confidentiality as differentiators. Its anecdotal reliability concerns and adoption incentives also reinforce the synthesis’s caution that displacement depends on governance, implementation and buyer economics rather than model access alone.
qs: There’s been a lot of talk about whether both are in danger of being replaced directly by Claude as Anthropic have released legal co-working tools themselves.
By contrast Legora and simiar are tailored to legal professionals within large law firms and corporate legal departments.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI should remain subject to informed human control, existing professional duties and context-specific disclosure. Its strongest direct contribution is anecdotal support for the concern that verification can offset some efficiency gains: AI may accelerate summarisation and duplication, but knowledgeable review is still needed. The separate pricing and employment comments are unsupported opinions and do not materially alter this overall alignment.
qs: This requires users of Generative AI to be guided by, and act in accordance with, their existing legal and professional responsibilities.[3] It follows that there will be circumstances where it is inappropriate to use Generative AI at all or where users ought to be transparent about its use.
I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.

kp.k: AI superiority claims rest on anonymous practitioner impressions
kp.d: The original poster claims that legal AI now surpasses teams in investigations, document review, litigation and regulatory work, including substantive analysis rather than merely administration, and extends the argument to transactions. The claimed improvement over the last 18 months is a personal assessment, not a reported comparative study; senior lawyers may still supply recommendations.
qs: It’s not just the administration of tedious volume activity - the insight and intelligence is there. The joining of dots and analysis.
The change in the last 18 months has been staggering.
Yes some senior and experienced mind may provide a gloss or recommendation on the work product

kp.k: Hourly economics face predicted ethical and competitive pressure
kp.d: The original poster characterises aggregated-hours billing as presumptively unethical, claims clients are being overcharged for 90%+ of work product, and predicts insolvency for firms that fail to change their value proposition. AI-enabled fixed fees are presented as the replacement. Another participant predicts that 95% of each chargeable pound disappears, while a dissenter challenges calling prices accepted by sophisticated clients a scam. These are contested opinions and projections.
qs: You are fleecing the client for 90%+ of the work product.
The fixed fee value proposition with AI driven cost and quality drivers will rip it all up.
The spread of tech and now AI means, very simply, that 95% of each chargeable £ disappears.
Can someone please tell my why it is a 'scam' for anyone to charge what the sophisticated business client/customer will pay for a service?

kp.k: Disruption timelines and employment consequences remain disputed
kp.d: The original poster anticipates market upheaval within 24 months and advises lawyers to join committed innovators, repositioning themselves as strategic business consultants with legal expertise. Another participant predicts most legal jobs will disappear or change substantially and fees will fall. A more cautious contributor places the major City-law tipping point closer to 10 years than two, citing errors and compliant data access, while allowing earlier disruption elsewhere.
qs: Be very concerned and be agile.
the lawyer is the strategic consultant - a specialist and highly qualified business consultant with a legal fine-tune.
Most law jobs are going to be lost, or significantly changed with a large reduction in the fees that can be charged.
So I would say the really big tipping point is probably closer to 10 years away than two. For city law anyway.

kp.k: Junior displacement threatens the future expertise pipeline
kp.d: The original poster predicts that a structure of juniors learning on the job beneath equity-owning seniors will fail as junior work disappears. A frequent AI user separately argues that experienced lawyers can detect AI mistakes because they learned through their own errors, but subsequent generations may lack that formative experience. The latter frames the risk around their retirement in approximately 15 years.
qs: The junior flow will dry up. The flow to mid and senior will not work right.
There will be a dearth of this elusive ‘experience’ that justifies the old model.
I learned that through making mistakes.
I’ll retire in 15 years or so.

kp.k: Confidentiality constrains otherwise broad workflow automation
kp.d: One participant describes Claude controlling a laptop to interrogate 100 SPAs, find party information and populate ancillary documents, but identifies confidentiality and client requirements as constraints. They allege unauthorised use at firms up to at least the mid-market and contrast it with transferring material into products such as Relativity or Harvey. A separate request dated 16 Apr 26 seeks factual-document analysis compliant with UK data protection and professional confidentiality.
qs: So if you had e.g. 100 SPAs saved on there you could quickly have it interrogating those for precedents, searching the internet for party details, populating ancillary documents etc.
The issue comes from confidentiality/client requirements.
Is anyone using anything of use which complies with UK data protection and client confidentiality rules applying to solicitors and bazzas?

kp.k: Data organisation underpins regulatory and transactional automation
kp.d: A participant argues that firms have failed to structure data, capture knowledge and apply project management. They see regulatory advice as particularly exposed where public legislation can be combined with accumulated private interpretations. Transactional work retains temporary protection from deadlines and disorganised inputs, but could move toward term-sheet-driven drafting with one human checking the result once precedents are organised.
qs: The reality is all law firms have largely been taking the piss out of clients for years through failing to structure data and comprehensively capture it, and implement standard project management techniques.
The main area for me where there seems to be no hope is regulatory advice.
you click the options on a term sheet and a computer with perhaps 1 person vetting it plugs exactly the correct terms into the agreement.

kp.k: Implementation requires workflow leadership, not merely software acquisition
kp.d: An anonymous practice-area AI implementation lead describes the task as making existing software produce useful legal outputs rather than developing software. Other contributors criticise superficial prompting and marketing-led adoption despite expenditure of millions. One names CC, Latham, Bakers and Simpson Thacher as firms that understand the opportunity, but offers no comparative evidence. The closing contribution stresses detailed instructions, supervision, investment and long-term organisational change.
qs: I’m “in charge” of getting it to produce what needs to be produced in a legal business.

There are several firms that have spent millions on AI tools and routinely bang on about their use for BD purposes, but it is mostly lawyers using 3 line one off prompts to do marginal stuff like doc comparison.
CC, Latham, Bakers, Simpson Thacher plus a few others.
realising this involves hard work and investment not waiting for the travelling salesperson to show up

kp.k: Anecdotal adoption includes explicit client demand
kp.d: One participant reports an imminent Legora trial and a client asking, during a pitch for large-volume document review, for confirmation that AI would be used. Another argues that technology-driven transactional review was possible for 10+ years with a couple of data scientists, presenting current uptake as belated rather than wholly dependent on new capabilities.
qs: We are just about to trial Legora and have also had a client ask us to confirm in a pitch for review large number of documents that we'll use AI for that.
They could have been doing tech driven transactional doc review for 10+ years with a couple of data scientists.

kp.k: Reported errors sustain demands for human verification
kp.d: Several participants dispute the original poster's dismissal of hallucinations. One reports reviewing another firm's apparently AI-generated reports containing poor material; another describes reversals of legal positions and considers human accuracy comparisons misleading. These are practitioner anecdotes, not measured error rates. Their position is that time savings in summarisation and duplication do not remove the need for competent human review.
qs: I have recently had the misfortune to review numerous reports prepared by another firm where they have clearly used AI and the output is full of guff.
a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.
Night equals day reversals of positions are common in a way they just aren’t in human produced stuff (in my experience at least).

kp.k: Multi-question analysis can compound early mistakes
kp.d: A frequent user describes a paid captive system as highly useful but reports a document-analysis exercise involving 10 questions: answers 1–4 were satisfactory, a mistake emerged at question 5, and subsequent output introduced material absent from the document. They recommend testing the same question through a clean prompt 2–3 times and carefully probing the initial response. Their explanation of error propagation is a user interpretation, not a technical finding.
qs: I’ve given it a doc and asked it to analyse on the basis of 10 questions.
Questions 1-4, perfect. Then a wobble at Q5, and then the wheels come off entirely.
It was telling my things that the document didn’t contain – adding in scenarios not analysed in the source material.
I’ve also found that you need to ask the same question via a “clean” prompt 2-3 times.

kp.k: Court guidance preserves responsibility and possible disclosure
kp.d: A sceptical participant quotes Australian Federal Court guidance to counter dismissal of AI risks. As reproduced in the thread, the guidance requires basic understanding of capabilities and limitations, consistency with existing legal and professional responsibilities, and disclosure if the court requires it; some uses may be inappropriate. This quoted institutional position differs from the original poster's prediction that courts and the judiciary will embrace AI rapidly.
qs: Any person who uses Generative AI will have a basic understanding of its capabilities, and its limitations and risks.
Any use of Generative AI must not adversely affect the administration of justice.
If the Court requires it, a person must disclose to the Court if (and how) Generative AI has been used in a proceeding.
The courts and judiciary will embrace it and outpace you.

kp.k: Regulatory protection and outsourcing may preserve lawyer roles
kp.d: Some participants assert that only humans can give legal advice and predict regulation will protect lawyers while productivity increases. Others respond that much billed advice is actually analysis or rearranged material susceptible to automation. A contributor allows that banks could insource work using AI but expects continued outsourcing for risk allocation; another envisages firms checking generated documents partly to access their insurance. The thread does not establish the legal scope of the asserted human-only restriction.
qs: Only humans can give legal advice, so until that changes we’re safe from our Anthropic overlords.
The reality is a heck of a lot of what lawyers now sell as "advice" is not advice but analysis and re-ordered review of material.
Maybe the banks will insource everything to in-house legal with ai, but my feeling is that they’d prefer to outsource still to law firms for risk purposes
which might be sent for checking to exploit a law firm's insurance policy.

kp.k: Bank spending creates buyer pressure for AI savings
kp.d: A participant claiming in-house experience reports managing a £750m litigation budget, with discovery and document management consuming substantial hourly fees; adverse-party costs and in-house headcount were additional. They predict CFO pressure will force GCs to obtain AI savings and banks will mandate adoption. This is an anonymous spending anecdote supporting a forecast, not independently substantiated market evidence.
qs: In my day in-house I ran a £750m budget on litigation alone.
Much of the costs I incurred were process around discovery and doc management.
any GC who can procure a saving like this will be forced to, by a CFO.
Banks are probably the most likely to mandate this.

kp.k: Bank-controlled precedent databases could standardise transactional production
kp.d: One contributor predicts banks will marshal their own and advisers' data to assemble model wording for virtually every agreed scenario, leaving negotiation at the margins. They envisage banks commissioning pan-European corporate authorisation and registration knowledge to generate ancillary documents for subsequent checking. This is a proposed pathway to automation, not a reported implementation.
qs: Large banks from a transactional perspective will wake up to marshalling their available data, and if they are clever will co-opt their closest advisers to give up theirs too to assist them.
Effectively you have an uber-ISDA for every work type and negotiation, if there is any, comes around the margins.

kp.k: Vendor differentiation and platform dependence are contested
kp.d: One poster distinguishes legal-specific Legora from general-purpose Claude and Copilot, reporting 800 customers and tens of thousands of daily users as of March 2026. Another characterises Legora as a Claude wrapper and Harvey as using ChatGPT, claims confidentiality is their main differentiation, and reports discussion of displacement by Anthropic's legal tools. These architectural, confidentiality and usage assertions are participants' claims, not verified vendor disclosures within the thread.
qs: 800 customers and tens of thousands of daily users as of March 2026.
The platform is primarily used for AI-powered legal research, document drafting, review, and collaboration on complex matters.
Legora is based on Claude (Anthropic).
Harvey is identical, but uses ChatGPT for their LLM.
There’s been a lot of talk about whether both are in danger of being replaced directly by Claude as Anthropic have released legal co-working tools themselves.

kp.k: Scale advantages could intensify competition downmarket
kp.d: A participant predicts that firms investing effectively in AI will expand without additional staff and compete progressively downmarket on value and scale. They argue that errors should be managed through designed guardrails rather than treated as grounds for abandoning automation, comparing poor AI implementation with failed outsourcing and delegation. Another draws a post-GFC analogy in which better-organised firms took work from lower market tiers.
qs: they likely don't need to hire any more staff and can come for work at their level and lower and lower down the foodchain.
a system that has guardrails and accepts imperfections as a bug that needs managed rather than removed
the organised top came for the middle and the organised middle came for the bottom

kp.k: Some welcome displacement as economic resource reallocation
kp.d: One participant explicitly welcomes AI replacing lawyers, depicting expenditure on legal documents and interpretation as a drag on productive activity and predicting graduates could move into medicine or technology development. This is a normative economic argument rather than evidence of realised benefits or improved access to justice.
qs: AI replacing lawyers would be hugely positive.
All the time and money that the country spends on legal docs/ interpretation is a drag on economically productive activity.
Bright grads will then abandon overpaid legal roles and do something more useful, like trying to find cures for diseases, or developing some new tech.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Participants predict substantial automation, fee compression, changes to staffing and competition, but disagree over the speed of substitution and the continuing importance of human verification and regulatory protection.
pts.d: The original anonymous poster claims that AI already surpasses legal teams in document-intensive investigation, litigation and regulatory work, with implications for transactions as well. They argue that aggregate-hours billing is becoming unjustifiable, predict disruption by AI-driven fixed-fee offerings and insolvency for firms that fail to adapt, and envisage lawyers becoming strategic consultants. They also predict a breakdown in the junior-to-senior training pipeline and judicial adoption that outpaces the Bar. A self-described practice-area AI implementation lead anticipates a major productivity increase. Other anonymous participants predict extensive job losses or role changes, cheaper access to expertise and sharply lower fees; one asserts that 95% of each chargeable pound will disappear. A transaction-focused participant anticipates automated precedent interrogation, ancillary-document production and term-sheet-driven agreements with perhaps one human checking them, while portraying regulatory advice as especially vulnerable once previously private interpretations can be aggregated. Another predicts that banks will consolidate transaction data into comprehensive model-document systems, retaining firms partly for checking and insurance. A competition-focused participant predicts that investing firms can expand into lower market segments without additional staff. Counterclaims include continued human verification, legal and regulatory protection for human advisers, increased professional productivity and wealth rather than collapse, and continued outsourcing to firms for risk allocation. A participant also raises the possibility that model providers' own legal tools will displace specialist legal-AI vendors.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The discussion relies predominantly on anonymous professional experience, observations and conjecture; it supplies no reproducible performance benchmarks or quantified labour-market evidence.
pts.d: The original poster grounds their claims in a recent examination of an unnamed platform, without identifying tasks tested, comparative measurements or error rates. Their 90%+ overcharging assertion and another participant's 95% fee-disappearance prediction have no supporting calculation. The self-described implementation lead offers a professional impression. A participant reports an imminent Legora trial and a client request to use AI in a large-document-review pitch: evidence of particular adoption intentions, not completed productivity results. A former in-house participant cites responsibility for a £750m litigation budget and substantial discovery/document-management spending as the basis for predicting bank demand. Another reports Legora having 800 customers and tens of thousands of daily users as of March 2026, but provides no accompanying citation. Critical experience includes allegedly AI-generated reports from another firm that required correction and a frequent user's account of an initially successful ten-question document analysis that subsequently invented material. The latter also reports needing repeated clean prompts and careful testing. A sceptical participant invokes an Australian Federal Court practice note requiring awareness of limitations and compliance with professional responsibilities; the quoted court text supports caution but does not provide measured error rates. Statements about particular firms' investment quality, vendor model architectures, confidentiality arrangements and regulatory exclusivity are participant assertions rather than independently established findings in this document.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2026 thread contrasts immediate or two-year disruption with a roughly ten-year tipping point for City law, conditional on reliability, compliant data access, investment, client acceptance and regulation.
pts.d: The original poster describes a dramatic improvement over the preceding 18 months and predicts market disruption within the next 24 months. Another participant says the staffing and fixed-fee changes are already present. A slower-change participant predicts that the major tipping point for City law is closer to ten years than two, with earlier disruption possible further down the market and faster progress where public datasets are abundant. Confidentiality and client requirements are repeatedly identified as current constraints; one participant says direct computer-use automation is technically possible but that firms may instead need controlled legal-AI products. Transactional work is described as temporarily protected by urgency and disorganised client data, until clients demand standardisation. A report-reviewing participant requires knowledgeable human verification, while the frequent user describes cascading errors and the need to probe responses. Regulatory-protection claims are expressly conditional on rules continuing to require human legal advice, as those participants understand them. Elite US adoption is framed as conditional on profitability. The final participant argues that effective deployment depends on adequate instructions, supervision, system design and sustained investment rather than simply buying software. The frequent user's retirement horizon of approximately 15 years frames concern about whether the next generation will retain the experience needed to check AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Predicted effects span junior employment and training, equity-partner economics, firm survival, corporate purchasing, legal-AI vendors and the distribution of skilled labour.
pts.d: The original poster identifies associates, trainees and paralegals doing document review and evidence extraction as immediately exposed, with senior lawyers retaining a strategic advisory role. They warn young lawyers against joining unadapted firms and mid-ranking lawyers against assuming that their careers or firms are secure. Multiple participants predict reduced junior recruitment and a weakened supply of experienced future lawyers; the frequent user specifically links lost learning-by-error opportunities to diminished ability to verify AI output. Traditional equity-partner firms and hours-based providers face predicted fee compression, restructuring or failure, while well-organised investing firms are expected to win work through lower costs and scale. A participant names CC, Latham, Bakers and Simpson Thacher as firms that understand the shift, without supplying investment evidence. Banks and their in-house legal departments are described as particularly strong buyers of automation because discovery and document-management costs are large and CFOs will pressure GCs to save money. Transaction advisers may lose drafting work while retaining checking and risk-bearing functions. Regulatory advisers are portrayed by one participant as especially exposed, whereas City transactional work is described by others as slower to substitute. The original poster predicts adoption by courts and the judiciary; a later question about discretionary judging does not receive a concrete answer. Legora and Harvey are discussed as software vendors serving law firms and corporate legal departments, with possible competitive pressure from underlying model providers. A participant welcoming replacement predicts that graduates will leave law for medicine-related research or technology development, presenting this as a broader economic benefit rather than as an evidenced labour-market outcome.
